metadata.title: Graph-directed systems and self-similar measures on limit spaces of self-similar groups

extraction_notes.note: Uncited background facts in the review sections (tile intersection criterion, characterization of Bernoulli measures, every action from a triple) typed as external claims rather than theorems because the paper does not name them.
Proposition 6 has no proof environment; the preceding paragraph (subset construction, 'similar to the proof of Theorem 3.3.2') is taken as its proof sketch, so the proposition is marked semi_formal.
Item 3 of Proposition 10 is proved separately and cited separately ('item~3 implies'); not split into nested claims because the \ref targets the whole proposition.

The paper's algorithms are described in running text and remarks (eigenvector computation, label product graph); extracted as unmarked algorithms with judgment-based steps, while the tile-intersection method stays a remark node.
The proof cites Theorem 11 as 'Proposition~\ref{theor_tile_measure}'; the ref resolves correctly to TP7.
Minor asides (closedness of $B_v$, $F_v$; spectral radius bounds; countability of contracting groups; Malcev-completion remark 'The same observation holds ...') were left in the running text.

nodes.name: self-similar set (attractor)
nodes.statement:
The self-similar set
(the attractor) given by the system of contracting similarities $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ (iterated function
system) of a complete metric space is the unique compact set $T$ satisfying $T=\cup_{i=1}^n
f_i(T)$.

nodes.name: Hutchinson's theorem on self-similar measures
nodes.statement:
Given a probability vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, Hutchinson
\cite{hutch:fract_self_similarity} showed the existence of a unique probability measure $\mu$
supported on $T$ satisfying
\begin{equation} \mu(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i\mu(f_i^{-1}(A)), \mbox{ for any Borel set $A$},
\end{equation}
which is called the self-similar measure.
nodes.statement_short: For an IFS with probability vector $p$ there is a unique probability measure on the attractor satisfying the self-similarity equation.
assumptions: Given a probability vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)$
conclusions: the existence of a unique probability measure $\mu$ supported on $T$ satisfying

nodes.name: Self-similarity equation for measures
nodes.statement: \mu(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i\mu(f_i^{-1}(A)), \mbox{ for any Borel set $A$},
nodes.label: eqn_self_similar_measure

nodes.name: finite words $X^*$
nodes.statement:
Denote by $X^{*}=\{x_1x_2\ldots x_n | x_i\in X,
n\geq 0\}$ the set of all finite words over $X$ (including the empty word denoted $\emptyset$).

nodes.name: right-infinite sequences $X^\omega$
nodes.statement:
Let
$X^{\omega}$ be the set of all right-infinite sequences (words) $x_1x_2\ldots$, $x_i\in X$.

nodes.name: left-infinite sequences $X^{-\omega}$
nodes.statement:
Let
$X^{-\omega}$ be the set of all left-infinite sequences (words) $\ldots x_2x_1$, $x_i\in X$.

nodes.name: length of a word
nodes.statement:
The length of a word $v=x_1x_2\ldots x_n$ is denoted by $|v| =
n$.

nodes.name: shift on $X^\omega$
nodes.statement:
The \textit{shift on the space $X^\omega$} is the map $\sigma:X^\omega\rightarrow X^\omega$, which deletes the
first letter of a word, i.e. $\sigma(x_1x_2x_3\ldots) = x_2x_3\ldots$.
differentia: deletes the first letter of a word

nodes.name: shift on $X^{-\omega}$
nodes.statement:
The \textit{shift on the
space $X^{-\omega}$} is the map also denoted by $\sigma$, which deletes the last letter of a word, i.e.
$\sigma(\ldots x_3x_2x_1) = \ldots x_3x_2$.
differentia: deletes the last letter of a word

nodes.name: inverse branches $\sigma_x$
nodes.statement:
The
branches $\sigma_x$ for $x\in X$ of the inverse of $\sigma$ are defined by
$\sigma_x(x_1x_2\ldots)=xx_1x_2\ldots$ and $\sigma_x(\ldots x_2x_1)=\ldots x_2x_1x$.

nodes.name: Bernoulli measure
nodes.statement:
Let $p=(p_x)_{x\in X}$ be a probability vector (fixed for the rest of the section) and let $\mu_p$
be the \textit{Bernoulli measure} on $X^\omega$ with weight $p$, i.e. this measure is defined on
cylindrical sets by
\[
\mu_p(x_1x_2\ldots x_nX^\omega)=p_{x_1}p_{x_2}\ldots p_{x_n}.
\]
nodes.statement_short: The Bernoulli measure $\mu_p$ with weight $p$ gives a cylinder $x_1\ldots x_nX^\omega$ measure $p_{x_1}\cdots p_{x_n}$.

nodes.name: uniform Bernoulli measure
nodes.statement:
In case $p_x=\frac{1}{|X|}$ for all $x\in X$,
the measure $\mu_p$ is the \textit{uniform Bernoulli measure} denoted $\mu_u$.

nodes.name: one-sided Bernoulli $|X|$-shift
nodes.statement:
The dynamical system
$(X^\omega,\sigma,\mu_u)$ is called the \textit{one-sided Bernoulli $|X|$-shift}.

nodes.name: Bernoulli measure characterized by self-similarity
nodes.statement:
The measure $\mu_p$ is
the unique regular Borel probability measure on $X^\omega$ that satisfies the self-similarity condition:
\[
\mu_p(A)=\sum_{x\in X} p_x\mu_p(\sigma_x^{-1}(A))
\]
for any Borel set $A\subset X^\omega$.
conclusions: The measure $\mu_p$ is the unique regular Borel probability measure on $X^\omega$ that satisfies the self-similarity condition

nodes.name: sequence starts in a vertex
nodes.statement:
Let
$\Gamma=(V,E)$ be such a graph and take a vertex $v\in V$. We say that a sequence $x_1x_2\ldots\in X^\omega$
(a word $x_1x_2\ldots x_n\in X^{*}$) \textit{starts in the vertex $v$} if there exists a
right-infinite path $e_1e_2\ldots$ (finite path $e_1e_2\ldots e_n$) in $\Gamma$, which starts in $v$
and is labeled by $x_1x_2\ldots$ (respectively $x_1x_2\ldots x_n$).

nodes.name: sequence ends in a vertex
nodes.statement:
Similarly, we say that a
sequence $\ldots x_2x_1\in X^{-\omega}$ (a word $x_n\ldots x_2x_1\in X^{*}$) \textit{ends in the vertex
$v$} if there exists a left-infinite path $\ldots e_2e_1$ (finite path $e_n\ldots e_2e_1$) in
$\Gamma$, which ends in $v$ and is labeled by $\ldots x_2x_1$ (respectively $x_n\ldots x_2x_1$).

nodes.name: vertex set $V(w)$
nodes.statement:
For
every $w\in X^*\cup X^{-\omega}$ denote by $V_\Gamma(w)=V(w)\subset V$ the set of all vertices $v\in V$ such
that the sequence $w$ ends in $v$.

nodes.name: monotonicity of $V(w)$
nodes.statement:
Observe that $V(w'w)\subseteq V(w)$ for arbitrary word $w'$ and
finite word~$w$.
assumptions: for arbitrary word $w'$ and finite word~$w$
conclusions: $V(w'w)\subseteq V(w)$

nodes.name: sets $B_v$ and $F_v$
nodes.statement:
For every vertex $v\in V$ denote by $B_v$ the set of all right-infinite sequences that start in
$v$, and denote by $F_v$ the set of all left-infinite sequences that end in $v$.

nodes.name: sofic subshifts
nodes.statement:
The sets
$\mathscr{B}=\cup_{v\in V}B_v$ and $\mathscr{F}=\cup_{v\in V}F_v$ are the one-sided (respectively, right and left)
\textit{sofic subshifts} associated with the graph $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: graph-directed recursion for $F_v$
nodes.statement:
The sets $F_v, v\in V$, satisfy the
recursion
\[
F_v=\bigcup_{u\, \stackrel{x}{\rightarrow} \,v} \sigma_x(F_u)
\]
(here the union is taken over all edges which end in $v$).
conclusions: The sets $F_v, v\in V$, satisfy the recursion

nodes.name: right-resolving graph
nodes.statement:
A labeled graph $\Gamma=(V,E)$ is called \textit{right-resolving} (Shannon graph in some terminology)
if for every vertex $v\in V$ the edges starting at $v$ have different labels.
differentia: for every vertex $v\in V$ the edges starting at $v$ have different labels

nodes.name: Every sofic subshift is given by a right-resolving graph
nodes.statement:
Every sofic subshift
can be given by a right-resolving graph (see Theorem~3.3.2 in \cite{IntroSymbDyn}).
conclusions: Every sofic subshift can be given by a right-resolving graph

nodes.name: strictly right-resolving graph
nodes.statement:
A
right-resolving graph is called \textit{strictly right-resolving} if every vertex $v\in V$ has an
outgoing edge labeled by $x$ for every $x\in X$.
differentia: every vertex $v\in V$ has an outgoing edge labeled by $x$ for every $x\in X$

nodes.name: measure vectors and $\mu_p(\Gamma)$
nodes.statement:
For a labeled graph $\Gamma=(V,E)$ we use the following notations:
\[
\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{B})=(\mu_p(B_v))_{v\in V}, \quad  \vec\mu_p(\mathscr{F})=(\mu_p(F_v))_{v\in V}, \quad \mbox{ and }
\quad \mu_p(\Gamma)=\sum_{v\in V} \mu_p(F_v).
\]

nodes.name: Measure number of a right-resolving graph is integer
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph. Then \[ \mu_p(\Gamma)=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|=\min_{w\in X^*} |V(w)|. \] In particular, the measure $\mu_p(\Gamma)$ is integer.
nodes.statement_short: For a finite right-resolving graph, $\mu_p(\Gamma)$ equals the minimal number of vertices a word ends in; hence it is an integer.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph.
conclusions: \mu_p(\Gamma)=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|=\min_{w\in X^*} |V(w)|.
In particular, the measure $\mu_p(\Gamma)$ is integer.
also_stated_at:
It is proved in
Section~\ref{section_Sofic} that if the graph $\Gamma$ is right-resolving (i.e. for every vertex $v$
the outgoing edges at $v$ are labeled distinctly) then the sum $meas(\Gamma)=\sum_{v\in V} \mu_p(F_v)$
is integer, which does not depend on the probability vector $p$.
nodes.label: theor_measure_graph_integer

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Let $w=\ldots x_2x_1\in X^{-\omega}$ and denote $w_n=x_n\ldots x_2x_1$ for $n\geq 1$. Observe, that $V(w)\subseteq V(w_n)$ and $V(w_n)\subseteq V(w_m)$ for $n\geq m$. Take a vertex $v\in \cap_{n\geq 1} V(w_n)$. Let $P_n$ be the set of all paths $e_n\ldots e_2e_1$ labeled by $w_n$ and ending in $v$. The set $P_n$ is a finite non-empty set for every $n$, and $e_{n-1}\ldots e_2e_1\in P_{n-1}$ for every path $e_n\ldots e_2e_1\in P_n$. Since the inverse limit of a sequence of finite non-empty sets is non-empty, there exists a left-infinite path $\ldots e_2e_1$ labeled by $w$ and ending in $v$. Then $v\in V(w)$ and we get \begin{equation} V(w)=\bigcap_{n\geq 1} V(w_n). \end{equation} From this follows that $|V(w)|=\min\limits_{n\geq 1} |V(w_n)|$ for $w\in X^{-\omega}$. Then \[ \min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} \min_{n\geq 1} |V(w_n)|=\min_{w\in X^*} |V(w)| \] and the second equality of the theorem is proved. Define the integer $k=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|$ and consider the set $\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}(\Gamma)\subseteq X^{-\omega}$ of all sequences $w\in X^{-\omega}$ such that $|V(w)|=k$. Define $\mathcal{O}^*$ as the set of finite words that satisfy the same condition. We have the following lemma. \begin{lemma} The set $\mathcal{O}$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}$, and $\mu_p(\mathcal{O})=1$. For each $w\in\mathcal{O}$ there is a beginning of $w$ that belongs to $\mathcal{O}^*$. Equivalently, $\mathcal{O}=\cup_{w\in\mathcal{O}^*}X^{-\omega} w$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} If $w\in\mathcal{O}$ then $k=|V(w)|=\min_{n\geq 1} |V(w_n)|$ and there exists $N\geq 1$ such that $|V(w_N)|=k$. Then $k\leq |V(\omega w_N)|\leq |V(w_N)|=k$ for all $\omega\in X^{-\omega}$. Hence $w_N\in\mathcal{O}^*$, $X^{-\omega} w_N\subseteq\mathcal{O}$ and so $\mathcal{O}$ is open, and thus measurable. Let $u\in X^*$ be such that $|V(u)|=k$. Let us show that if $w\in X^{-\omega}$ contains the subword $u$ then $w\in\mathcal{O}$. If $w=w'u$ then $k\leq |V(w'u)|\leq |V(u)|=k$ and $w\in\mathcal{O}$. Observe that $V(ux)$ is the set of those vertices $v\in V$ for which there exists an edge labeled by $x$ which starts in some vertex of $V(u)$ and ends in $v$. Since the graph $\Gamma$ is right-resolving there is no more than one such an edge for each vertex of $V(u)$, and thus $|V(ux)|\leq |V(u)|$. It implies that if $w=w'uu'$ than $k\leq |V(w)|\leq |V(u)|=k$ and thus $|V(w)|=k$, so $w\in\mathcal{O}$. The Bernoulli measure of the set of all words $w'uu', u'\in X^*, w'\in X^{-\omega}$, is equal to $1$. Thus $\mu_p(\mathcal{O})=1$. It follows also that $\mathcal{O}$ is dense in $X^{-\omega}$. \end{proof} By construction of the set $\mathcal{O}$ for every $w\in\mathcal{O}$ there exist exactly $k$ vertices $v$ such that $w\in F_v$. Let $\chi_{F_v}$ be the characteristic function of the set $F_v$. Then $\sum_{v\in V}\chi_{F_v}=k$ almost everywhere. Integrating we get $\mu_p(\Gamma)=\sum\limits_{v\in V} \mu_p(F_v)=k$.
nodes.statement_short: Inverse-limit (Konig) argument gives $V(w)=\cap_n V(w_n)$; then the set $\mathcal{O}$ of minimizing sequences has full measure, and integrating the counting function gives $k$.

nodes.name: $V(w)$ as intersection of $V(w_n)$
nodes.statement: V(w)=\bigcap_{n\geq 1} V(w_n).
nodes.label: eqn_th1_V(w) eq cap V(w_n)

nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{O}$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}$, and $\mu_p(\mathcal{O})=1$. For each $w\in\mathcal{O}$ there is a beginning of $w$ that belongs to $\mathcal{O}^*$. Equivalently, $\mathcal{O}=\cup_{w\in\mathcal{O}^*}X^{-\omega} w$.
nodes.statement_short: Sequences ending in the minimal number $k$ of vertices form an open dense set of full Bernoulli measure, determined by finite prefixes.
conclusions: The set $\mathcal{O}$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}$, and $\mu_p(\mathcal{O})=1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: If $w\in\mathcal{O}$ then $k=|V(w)|=\min_{n\geq 1} |V(w_n)|$ and there exists $N\geq 1$ such that $|V(w_N)|=k$. Then $k\leq |V(\omega w_N)|\leq |V(w_N)|=k$ for all $\omega\in X^{-\omega}$. Hence $w_N\in\mathcal{O}^*$, $X^{-\omega} w_N\subseteq\mathcal{O}$ and so $\mathcal{O}$ is open, and thus measurable. Let $u\in X^*$ be such that $|V(u)|=k$. Let us show that if $w\in X^{-\omega}$ contains the subword $u$ then $w\in\mathcal{O}$. If $w=w'u$ then $k\leq |V(w'u)|\leq |V(u)|=k$ and $w\in\mathcal{O}$. Observe that $V(ux)$ is the set of those vertices $v\in V$ for which there exists an edge labeled by $x$ which starts in some vertex of $V(u)$ and ends in $v$. Since the graph $\Gamma$ is right-resolving there is no more than one such an edge for each vertex of $V(u)$, and thus $|V(ux)|\leq |V(u)|$. It implies that if $w=w'uu'$ than $k\leq |V(w)|\leq |V(u)|=k$ and thus $|V(w)|=k$, so $w\in\mathcal{O}$. nodes.statement_short: Directly: a minimizing prefix forces minimality (openness); right-resolving makes $|V|$ non-increasing, and almost every sequence contains a given word.

nodes.name: Theorem 1 beyond Bernoulli measures
nodes.statement: The theorem holds not only for Bernoulli measures. The only property that was used is that for every word $u\in X^{*}$ the set of all words, which contain $u$ as a subword, has measure $1$. It should be pointed out that the number $\mu(\Gamma)$ is independent on the chosen measure $\mu$, while the measures $\mu(F_v)$, $\mu(B_v)$ and $\sum_{v\in V} \mu(B_v)$ depend on $\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1 only needs that sequences containing any fixed word have full measure; $\mu(\Gamma)$ is measure-independent.

nodes.name: measure number of a graph
nodes.statement: The number $meas(\Gamma)=\mu_p(\Gamma)$ is called the \textit{measure number} of the graph~$\Gamma$.
also_stated_at:
The number
$meas(\Gamma)$ we call the measure number of the graph $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Almost every sequence ends in $meas(\Gamma)$ vertices
nodes.statement:
Theorem~\ref{theor_measure_graph_integer} shows that almost every sequence $w\in X^{-\omega}$ ends in
precisely $meas(\Gamma)$ vertices of $\Gamma$.
conclusions: almost every sequence $w\in X^{-\omega}$ ends in precisely $meas(\Gamma)$ vertices of $\Gamma$

nodes.name: Full right and left sofic subshifts coincide
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite labeled graph. Then $\mathscr{B}=X^\omega$ if and only if $\mathscr{F}=X^{-\omega}$. In particular, $\mathscr{F}=X^{-\omega}$ for a finite strictly right-resolving graph $\Gamma$.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite labeled graph.
conclusions: $\mathscr{B}=X^\omega$ if and only if $\mathscr{F}=X^{-\omega}$
$\mathscr{F}=X^{-\omega}$ for a finite strictly right-resolving graph $\Gamma$
nodes.label: prop cup B_v eq cup F_v

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: Since the inverse limit of nonempty finite sets is nonempty, $\mathscr{B}=X^\omega$ ($\mathscr{F}=X^{-\omega}$) is equivalent to the fact that every finite word $v\in{X^*}$ labels some path in $\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: By compactness (inverse limit of nonempty finite sets), both conditions mean every finite word labels a path.

nodes.name: adjacency matrix
nodes.statement:
The matrix $A=(a_{vu})_{v,u\in V}$, where $a_{vu}$ is equal to the number of edges from $v$ to $u$,
is the \textit{adjacency matrix} of the graph $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: matrix $T_p$
nodes.statement:
For the probability vector $p=(p_x)_{x\in X}$
define the matrix
\[
T_p=(t_{vu})_{v,u\in V}, \mbox{ where } t_{vu}=\sum\limits_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u}p_x
\]
(the sum is taken over all edges from $v$ to $u$).

nodes.name: transition matrix
nodes.statement:
If the graph $\Gamma$ is right-resolving, then the
matrix $T_p$ is the \textit{transition matrix} of the random walk on the weighted directed graph
$\Gamma$, where each edge labeled by $x$ has weight $p_x$.

nodes.name: Measure vectors are eigenvectors of the transition matrix
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph with the transition matrix~$T_p$. If the vector $\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ is nonzero then it is the right eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue~$1$. If the vector $\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ is nonzero then it is the left eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue~$1$.
nodes.statement_short: For right-resolving graphs, nonzero $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ and $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ are right/left eigenvectors of $T_p$ for eigenvalue 1.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph with the transition matrix~$T_p$.
If the vector $\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ is nonzero
If the vector $\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ is nonzero
conclusions: it is the right eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue~$1$
it is the left eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue~$1$

assumptions: If the vector $\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ is nonzero
conclusions: it is the right eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue~$1$

assumptions: If the vector $\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ is nonzero
conclusions: it is the left eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue~$1$

nodes.label: prop_eigenvect_transition_matr

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: By construction, for every vertex $v\in V$ we have \[ B_v=\bigsqcup_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u} xB_u \] (here the union is disjoint because the graph $\Gamma$ is right-resolving). It implies \[ \mu_p(B_v)=\sum_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u} p_x\mu_p(B_{u})=\sum_{u\in V} t_{vu}\mu_p(B_{u}). \] Thus the nonzero vector $\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ is the right eigenvector of $T_p$ for the eigenvalue~$1$. Similarly, \[ F_v=\bigcup_{u\stackrel{x}\rightarrow v} F_{u}x,\ v\in V, \] and, since the graph $\Gamma$ is right-resolving, that implies \begin{equation*} \mu_p(F_v)\leq\sum_{u\stackrel{x}\rightarrow v} p_x\mu_p(F_{u})=\sum_{u\in V} t_{uv}\mu_p(F_{u})\quad \Rightarrow\quad \vec \mu_p(\mathscr{F})\leq\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{F}) T_p. \end{equation*} The standard arguments based on the theory of nonnegative matrices (see for example \cite[proof of Theorem 4.5]{he_hui:self_affine}, \cite[p. 197]{gab_yu:natur_til}, \cite{handbook:rothblum}) end the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $B_v$ and $F_v$ along edges to get the eigen-equation and an inequality, then conclude by Perron-Frobenius theory of nonnegative matrices.

nodes.name: Measure number is additive over terminal components
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph. Let $\{\Gamma_i\}$ be the set of all strongly connected components of $\Gamma$, which are strictly right-resolving graphs. Then $meas(\Gamma)=\sum_imeas(\Gamma_i)$.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph.
Let $\{\Gamma_i\}$ be the set of all strongly connected components of $\Gamma$, which are strictly right-resolving graphs.
conclusions: $meas(\Gamma)=\sum_imeas(\Gamma_i)$.
nodes.label: cor_meas_sum_meas

nodes.name: Open set condition for graphs gives measure number 1
nodes.statement:
In particular, if a finite strictly right-resolving graph $\Gamma$ contains a vertex $v_0$ such that
for each vertex $v$ there is a path in $\Gamma$ from $v$ to $v_0$ and for each $x\in X$ there is an
edge from $v_0$ to $v_0$ labeled by $x$ (the open set condition for graphs), then $meas(\Gamma)=1$.
assumptions: a finite strictly right-resolving graph $\Gamma$ contains a vertex $v_0$ such that for each vertex $v$ there is a path in $\Gamma$ from $v$ to $v_0$ and for each $x\in X$ there is an edge from $v_0$ to $v_0$ labeled by $x$
conclusions: $meas(\Gamma)=1$

nodes.name: Uniform measure vectors are eigenvectors of the adjacency matrix
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph with the adjacency matrix~$A$. For the uniform Bernoulli measure $\mu_u$ the nonzero vectors $\vec \mu_u(\mathscr{B})$ and $\vec \mu_u(\mathscr{F})$ are respectively the right and left eigenvectors of $A$ for the eigenvalue $|X|$.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite right-resolving graph with the adjacency matrix~$A$.
conclusions: For the uniform Bernoulli measure $\mu_u$ the nonzero vectors $\vec \mu_u(\mathscr{B})$ and $\vec \mu_u(\mathscr{F})$ are respectively the right and left eigenvectors of $A$ for the eigenvalue $|X|$.

nodes.name: Non-right-resolving graph with non-integer measure
nodes.statement: For the graph $\Gamma$ shown in Figure~\ref{fig_Example_3_Graphs} we get $F_a=X^{-\omega} 0$, $F_b=X^{-\omega}$, the vector $\vec\mu_u(\mathscr{F})=(1/2,1)$ is not an eigenvector of the adjacency matrix, and $\mu_u(\Gamma)=3/2$.

nodes.name: Same transition matrix, different measure numbers
nodes.statement: Consider two graphs $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ shown in Figure~\ref{fig_Example_3_Graphs}. They have the same transition matrix (for the uniform Bernoulli measure), however $F_{a_1}=F_{b_1}=X^{-\omega}$ and $F_{a_2}=X^{-\omega} 0$, $F_{b_2}=X^{-\omega} 1$. Hence, $\mu_u(\Gamma_1)=2$ and $\mu_u(\Gamma_2)=1$.

nodes.name: Reduction to strictly right-resolving components
nodes.statement:
It follows from
Proposition~\ref{prop_eigenvect_transition_matr} that the problem of finding $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ and
$\mu_p(\Gamma)$ reduces to the strongly connected components which are strictly right-resolving graphs
(for all other vertices $\mu_p(F_v)=0$).
conclusions: the problem of finding $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ and $\mu_p(\Gamma)$ reduces to the strongly connected components which are strictly right-resolving graphs

nodes.name: Normalized $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ is the stationary distribution
nodes.statement:
Notice that if $\Gamma$ is a strongly connected strictly
right-resolving graph, then the vector $\frac{1}{\mu_p(\Gamma)}\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ is the unique
stationary probability distribution of the stochastic matrix $T_p$.
assumptions: $\Gamma$ is a strongly connected strictly right-resolving graph
conclusions: the vector $\frac{1}{\mu_p(\Gamma)}\vec \mu_p(\mathscr{F})$ is the unique stationary probability distribution of the stochastic matrix $T_p$

nodes.name: Computing $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ for right-resolving graphs
nodes.statement:
At the same time Proposition~\ref{prop_eigenvect_transition_matr} implies the algorithm to find the
vector $\vec\mu_p(\mathscr{B})$ for a right-resolving graph. Indeed, a left eigenvector of $T_p$ for the
eigenvalue $1$ is uniquely defined if we know its entries $\mu_p(B_v)$ for vertices $v$ in the
strongly connected components of $\Gamma$ without outgoing edges. For every such a component $\Gamma'$,
we have $B_v=X^\omega$ and $\mu_p(B_v)=1$ for every vertex $v\in\Gamma'$ if the component $\Gamma'$ is a
strictly right-resolving graph, and $\mu_p(B_v)=0$ otherwise. In particular, if the matrix $T_p$ is
rational then the values $\mu_p(B_v)$ are rational.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the eigenvector equation of $T_p$ with boundary values 1 or 0 on terminal strongly connected components.

nodes.name: Boundary values on terminal components
nodes.statement:
For every such a component $\Gamma'$,
we have $B_v=X^\omega$ and $\mu_p(B_v)=1$ for every vertex $v\in\Gamma'$ if the component $\Gamma'$ is a
strictly right-resolving graph, and $\mu_p(B_v)=0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the entries on terminal components: 1 if strictly right-resolving, else 0.

nodes.name: Solve eigenvector equation
nodes.statement:
Indeed, a left eigenvector of $T_p$ for the
eigenvalue $1$ is uniquely defined if we know its entries $\mu_p(B_v)$ for vertices $v$ in the
strongly connected components of $\Gamma$ without outgoing edges.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to the unique eigenvector of $T_p$ for eigenvalue 1.

nodes.name: Measure problems for $B_v$ and $F_v$ are equivalent
nodes.statement:
Given a finite labeled graph $\Gamma=(V,E)$ the problems of finding the measures $\mu_p(B_v)$ and
$\mu_p(F_v)$ are equivalent, and can be reduced to right-resolving graphs.
assumptions: Given a finite labeled graph $\Gamma=(V,E)$
conclusions: the problems of finding the measures $\mu_p(B_v)$ and $\mu_p(F_v)$ are equivalent, and can be reduced to right-resolving graphs

nodes.name: Sketch of proof of Proposition 6 (subset construction)
nodes.statement:
The problem is that the
system
\[
B_v=\bigcup_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u} xB_{u}=\bigsqcup_{x\in
X}x\left(\bigcup_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u} B_{u}\right),\ v\in V
\]
is not self-similar in the sense that the above expression involves not only the sets $B_v$ but
also their finite unions. Introducing additional terms to this recursion corresponding to these
unions we get a system with a right-resolving graph. This procedure is similar to the construction
described in the proof of Theorem~3.3.2 in \cite{IntroSymbDyn}.
nodes.statement_short: Subset construction: add vertices for finite unions of the $B_u$ so the recursion becomes right-resolving, as in Lind-Marcus Thm 3.3.2.

nodes.name: The recursion for $B_v$ involves unions, so is not self-simi
nodes.statement:
The problem is that the
system
\[
B_v=\bigcup_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u} xB_{u}=\bigsqcup_{x\in
X}x\left(\bigcup_{v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u} B_{u}\right),\ v\in V
\]
is not self-similar in the sense that the above expression involves not only the sets $B_v$ but
also their finite unions.
nodes.statement_short: The recursion for $B_v$ involves unions, so is not self-similar.

nodes.name: Add vertices for the unions, giving a right-resolving graph.
nodes.statement:
Introducing additional terms to this recursion corresponding to these
unions we get a system with a right-resolving graph. This procedure is similar to the construction
described in the proof of Theorem~3.3.2 in \cite{IntroSymbDyn}.
nodes.statement_short: Add vertices for the unions, giving a right-resolving graph.

nodes.name: Right-resolving presentation of the sets $B_v$
nodes.statement: For every finite graph $\Gamma=(V,E)$ one can construct a finite right-resolving graph $\Gamma'=(V',E')$ with the property that for every $v\in V$ there exists $v'\in V'$ such that $B_v=B_{v'}$.
assumptions: For every finite graph $\Gamma=(V,E)$
conclusions: one can construct a finite right-resolving graph $\Gamma'=(V',E')$ with the property that for every $v\in V$ there exists $v'\in V'$ such that $B_v=B_{v'}$

nodes.name: Measures of the subshifts themselves
nodes.statement:
Similarly, one can find the measures of subshifts $\mathscr{B}$ and $\mathscr{F}$ by introducing new vertices
corresponding to $\cup_{v\in V} B_v$ and $\cup_{v\in V} F_v$.

nodes.name: Rationality of uniform measures of graph sets
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite labeled graph. For the uniform Bernoulli measure $\mu_u$ all measures $\mu_u(B_v)$, $\mu_u(F_v)$, $\mu_u(\Gamma)$ are rational.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$ be a finite labeled graph.
conclusions: For the uniform Bernoulli measure $\mu_u$ all measures $\mu_u(B_v)$, $\mu_u(F_v)$, $\mu_u(\Gamma)$ are rational.
nodes.label: cor_meas_gr_rational

nodes.name: Measure of $B_v\cap B_u$ via label product graph
nodes.statement:
Consider the question how to find the measure of the intersection $B_v\cap B_u$ for $v,u\in V$.
Construct a new graph $\mathscr{G}$ with the set of vertices $V\times V$ and put an edge from
$(v,u)$ to $(v',u')$ labeled by $x\in X$ for every edges $v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow v'$ and
$u\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u'$ in the graph $\Gamma$ (label products of graphs by Definition~3.4.8 in
\cite{IntroSymbDyn}). It is easy to see that then $B_{(v,u)}=B_v\cap B_u$ (see Proposition~3.4.10
in \cite{IntroSymbDyn}).
nodes.statement_short: Build the label product graph on $V\times V$; its sets $B_{(v,u)}$ are the intersections $B_v\cap B_u$.
output: the measure of the intersection $B_v\cap B_u$

nodes.name: Build label product graph
nodes.statement:
Construct a new graph $\mathscr{G}$ with the set of vertices $V\times V$ and put an edge from
$(v,u)$ to $(v',u')$ labeled by $x\in X$ for every edges $v\stackrel{x}\rightarrow v'$ and
$u\stackrel{x}\rightarrow u'$ in the graph $\Gamma$ (label products of graphs by Definition~3.4.8 in
\cite{IntroSymbDyn}).
nodes.statement_short: Construct the label product graph on $V\times V$.

nodes.name: Read off $B_{(v,u)}=B_v\cap B_u$
nodes.statement:
It is easy to see that then $B_{(v,u)}=B_v\cap B_u$ (see Proposition~3.4.10
in \cite{IntroSymbDyn}).
nodes.statement_short: Its vertex sets are the intersections, measured by the previous methods.

nodes.name: Graphs labeled by words
nodes.statement:
The described methods work in a more general case when labels are words over $X$. Let $\Gamma=(V,E)$
be a directed graph labeled by labels from $X^{*}\setminus\{\emptyset\}$. Define the sets $B_v$ and
$F_v$ for $v\in V$ as above. Similarly, the collection of sets $\{B_v, v\in V\}$ can be seen as the
graph-directed function system with the underlying graph $\Gamma$, where the map $\sigma_{x_1\ldots
x_n}=\sigma_{x_n}\circ\ldots\circ\sigma_{x_1}$ is associated with every edge labeled by $x_1\ldots
x_n$. To find the measures of the sets $B_v$ and $F_v$, we can replace each edge labeled by a word
$x_1x_2\ldots x_k$ by a sequence of edges labeled by letters $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k$, and apply the
above method to this new graph. Also we can directly use
Proposition~\ref{prop_eigenvect_transition_matr}, where such graph $\Gamma$ is called
\textit{right-resolving} if for every vertex $v\in V$ the word-label of an edge starting at $v$ is
not a prefix of the word-label of another edge starting at $v$ (i.e. in some sense the associated
automaton is deterministic). The transition matrix $T_p$ is defined similarly
\[
T_p=(t_{vu})_{v,u\in V}, \mbox{ where } t_{vu}=\sum\limits_{v\xrightarrow{x_1...x_k}
u}p_{x_1}p_{x_2}\ldots p_{x_k}.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Word-labeled graphs: subdivide edges into letters, or use Proposition 3 with prefix-free right-resolving and a product-weight transition matrix.

nodes.name: self-similar action
nodes.statement:
A faithful action of a group $G$ on the set $X^*$ is called
\emph{self-similar} if for every $g\in G$ and $x\in X$ there exist $h\in G$ and $y\in X$ such that
\[
g(xw)=yh(w)
\]
for all $w\in X^*$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.genus: A faithful action of a group $G$ on the set $X^*$
differentia: for every $g\in G$ and $x\in X$ there exist $h\in G$ and $y\in X$ such that

nodes.name: restriction $g|_x$
nodes.statement:
The element $h$ is called the \textit{restriction} of $g$ on $x$ and denoted
$h=g|_x$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: restriction on words
nodes.statement:
Inductively one defines the restriction $g|_{x_1x_2\ldots x_n}=g|_{x_1}|_{x_2}\ldots
|_{x_n}$ for every word $x_1\ldots x_n\in X^n$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: virtual endomorphism
nodes.statement:
The study of the self-similar actions of a group is in some sense
the study of the \textit{virtual endomorphisms} of this group, which are homomorphisms from a
subgroup of finite index to the group.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
differentia: from a subgroup of finite index to the group

nodes.name: coset transversal and cocycle
nodes.statement:
Let us choose a
left coset transversal $T=\{g_0,g_1,\ldots,g_{d-1}\}$ for the subgroup $H$, and a sequence
$C=\{h_0,h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}\}$ of elements of $G$ called a \emph{cocycle}.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: self-similar action defined by a triple $(\phi,T,C)$
nodes.statement:
The self-similar action
$(G,X^{*})$ with the alphabet $X=\{x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1}\}$ defined by the triple $(\phi,T,C)$ is
given by
\[
g(x_i)=x_j,\qquad g|_{x_i}=h_j^{-1}\phi(g_j^{-1}gg_i)h_i,
\]
where $j$ is such that $g_j^{-1}gg_i\in H$ (such $j$ is unique).
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.definiendum: self-similar action defined by the triple $(\phi,T,C)$
nodes.statement_short: The triple $(\phi,T,C)$ defines a self-similar action on $X^*$ by permuting letters via cosets and restricting through $\phi$.

nodes.name: Every self-similar action comes from a triple
nodes.statement: Conversely, every self-similar action can be obtained in this way.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
conclusions: every self-similar action can be obtained in this way

nodes.name: virtual endomorphism associated to a self-similar action
nodes.statement:
Then the map $\phi_x: g\mapsto g|_x$ is a
homomorphism from $St_G(x)$ to $G$ called \emph{the virtual endomorphism associated to the
self-similar action}.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.definiendum: the virtual endomorphism associated to the self-similar action

nodes.name: Actions with the same virtual endomorphism are conjugate
nodes.statement:
Different self-similar
actions of the group $G$ with the same associated virtual endomorphism are conjugated by
Proposition~2.3.4 in \cite{self_sim_groups}.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
assumptions: Different self-similar actions of the group $G$ with the same associated virtual endomorphism
conclusions: are conjugated

nodes.name: contracting self-similar action
nodes.statement:
A self-similar action of a group $G$ is called \emph{contracting} if there
exists a finite set $\mathcal{N}$ such that for every $g\in G$ there exists $k\in\mathbb{N}$ such that
$g|_v\in\mathcal{N}$ for all words $v\in X^*$ of length $\geq k$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.genus: A self-similar action of a group $G$
differentia: there exists a finite set $\mathcal{N}$ such that for every $g\in G$ there exists $k\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $g|_v\in\mathcal{N}$ for all words $v\in X^*$ of length $\geq k$

nodes.name: nucleus
nodes.statement:
The smallest set $\mathcal{N}$ with this
property is called the \emph{nucleus} of the self-similar action.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.genus: The smallest set $\mathcal{N}$ with this property

nodes.name: Moore diagram
nodes.statement:
It can be
represented by the \textit{Moore diagram}, which is the directed labeled graph with the set of
vertices $\mathcal{N}$, where there is an edge from $g$ to $g|_x$ labeled $(x,g(x))$ for every $x\in X$
and $g\in\mathcal{N}$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
differentia: with the set of vertices $\mathcal{N}$, where there is an edge from $g$ to $g|_x$ labeled $(x,g(x))$ for every $x\in X$ and $g\in\mathcal{N}$

nodes.name: asymptotic equivalence
nodes.statement:
Two elements $\ldots x_2x_1\cdot g$ and $\ldots
y_2y_1\cdot h$ of $X^{-\omega}\times G$ are called \textit{asymptotically equivalent} if there exist a
finite set $K\subset G$ and  a sequence $g_n\in K, n\geq 1,$ such that
\begin{displaymath}
g_n(x_n x_{n-1}\ldots x_1)=y_n y_{n-1}\ldots y_1\qquad \mbox{ and }\qquad g_n|_{x_n x_{n-1}\ldots
x_1}\cdot g=h
\end{displaymath}
for every $n\geq 1$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.statement_short: Two sequences with group elements are asymptotically equivalent if a bounded sequence of group elements maps one to the other on every finite suffix.

nodes.name: Asymptotic equivalence via paths in the nucleus
nodes.statement: Two elements $\ldots x_2x_1\cdot g$ and $\ldots y_2y_1\cdot h$ of $X^{-\omega}\times G$ are asymptotically equivalent if and only if there exists a left-infinite path $\ldots e_2e_1$ in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ ending in the vertex $hg^{-1}$ such that the edge $e_i$ is labeled by $(x_i,y_i)$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
conclusions: Two elements $\ldots x_2x_1\cdot g$ and $\ldots y_2y_1\cdot h$ of $X^{-\omega}\times G$ are asymptotically equivalent if and only if there exists a left-infinite path $\ldots e_2e_1$ in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ ending in the vertex $hg^{-1}$ such that the edge $e_i$ is labeled by $(x_i,y_i)$.
equivalent_conditions: Two elements $\ldots x_2x_1\cdot g$ and $\ldots y_2y_1\cdot h$ of $X^{-\omega}\times G$ are asymptotically equivalent
there exists a left-infinite path $\ldots e_2e_1$ in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ ending in the vertex $hg^{-1}$ such that the edge $e_i$ is labeled by $(x_i,y_i)$
nodes.label: prop_asympt_Moore_diagr

nodes.name: limit $G$-space
nodes.statement:
The quotient of the set $X^{-\omega}\times G$ by the asymptotic equivalence relation is called the
\textit{limit $G$-space} of the action and denoted $\limGs[(G,X^*)]$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: maps $\tau_x$
nodes.statement:
The map $\tau_x$ defined by the formula
\[
\tau_x(\ldots x_2 x_1\cdot g)=\ldots x_2 x_1 g(x)\cdot g|_x
\]
is a well-defined continuous map on the limit $G$-space $\limGs$ for every $x\in X$, which is not a
homeomorphism in general.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: maps $\tau_v$ for words
nodes.statement:
Inductively one defines $\tau_{x_1x_2\ldots
x_n}=\tau_{x_n}\circ\tau_{x_{n-1}}\circ\ldots\circ\tau_{x_1}$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: digit tile $\mathscr{T}$
nodes.statement: The image of $X^{-\omega}\times 1$ in $\limGs$ is called the \textit{(digit) tile} $\mathscr{T}$ of the action.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: tiles $\mathscr{T}_v$
nodes.statement:
The image of $X^{-\omega} v\times 1$ for $v\in X^n$ is called the \textit{tile} $\mathscr{T}_v$, equivalently
$\mathscr{T}_v=\tau_v(\mathscr{T})$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Intersecting tiles and the nucleus
nodes.statement: Two tiles $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ and $\mathscr{T}\cdot h$ intersect if and only if $gh^{-1}\in\mathcal{N}$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
conclusions: Two tiles $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ and $\mathscr{T}\cdot h$ intersect if and only if $gh^{-1}\in\mathcal{N}$.

nodes.name: open set condition
nodes.statement:
A
contracting action $(G,X^*)$ satisfies the \emph{open set condition} if for any element $g$ of the
nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ there exists a word $v\in X^*$ such that $g|_v=1$, i.e. in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$
there is a path from any vertex to the trivial state.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: Tiles under the open set condition
nodes.statement:
If the action satisfies the open set
condition then the tile $\mathscr{T}$ is the closure of its interior, and any two different tiles have
disjoint interiors; otherwise every tile $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ is covered by the other tiles (see
Proposition~3.3.7 in \cite{self_sim_groups}).
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
assumptions: If the action satisfies the open set condition
conclusions: the tile $\mathscr{T}$ is the closure of its interior, and any two different tiles have disjoint interiors
otherwise every tile $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ is covered by the other tiles

nodes.name: Limit $G$-space depends only on the virtual endomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $\phi: H\rightarrow G$ be a virtual endomorphism of the group $G$. Let $(G,X^*)$ and $(G,Y^*)$ be the contracting self-similar actions defined respectively by the triples $(\phi,T,C)$ and $(\phi,T',C')$. Then $\limGs[(G,X^*)]$ and $\limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ are homeomorphic and the homeomorphism is the map $\alpha : \limGs[(G,X^*)] \longrightarrow \limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ such that \[ \alpha(\tau_x(t))=\tau_y(\alpha(t))\cdot s_x,\ \mbox{ for }\ t\in \limGs[(G,X^*)], \] where $s_x={h'}_y^{-1}\phi({g'}_y^{-1}g_x)h_x$ and $y$ is such that $g'_yg_x^{-1}\in H$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.statement_short: Limit $G$-spaces of actions from triples with the same virtual endomorphism are homeomorphic via an explicit map $\alpha$ intertwining the $\tau_x$.
assumptions: Let $\phi: H\rightarrow G$ be a virtual endomorphism of the group $G$.
Let $(G,X^*)$ and $(G,Y^*)$ be the contracting self-similar actions defined respectively by the triples $(\phi,T,C)$ and $(\phi,T',C')$.
conclusions: Then $\limGs[(G,X^*)]$ and $\limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ are homeomorphic
nodes.label: theor_limsX hom limsY

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9 (by citation)
nodes.statement: The statement follows from Sections~2.1--2.5 in \cite{self_sim_groups}.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.statement_short: Cites Nekrashevych, Sections 2.1-2.5.

nodes.name: limit space
nodes.statement:
The factor of the limit $G$-space $\limGs$ by the action of the
group $G$ is called the \textit{limit space} $\lims=\lims(\phi)$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: shift map $\mathsf{s}$ on the limit space
nodes.statement:
The equivalence relation on $X^{-\omega}$ is invariant under the shift $\sigma$, therefore $\sigma$
induces a continuous surjective map $\mathsf{s}:\lims\rightarrow\lims$, and every point of $\lims$ has at
most $|X|$ preimages under $\mathsf{s}$.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: limit dynamical system
nodes.statement:
The dynamical system $(\lims,\mathsf{s})$ is called the \textit{limit
dynamical system} of the self-similar action.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces

nodes.name: tiles $\mathsf{T}_v$ of the limit space
nodes.statement:
The image of $X^{-\omega} v$ for $v\in X^{n}$ in $\lims$ is called the \textit{tile} $\mathsf{T}_v$ of the $n$-th
level.

nodes.name: Diameters of level-$n$ tiles tend to zero
nodes.statement: \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \max_{v\in X^n} \rm{diam} (\mathsf{T}_v)=0

nodes.name: limit solenoid
nodes.statement:
The inverse limit of the topological spaces $\lims\stackrel{\mathsf{s}}{\leftarrow} \lims
\stackrel{\mathsf{s}}{\leftarrow} \cdots$ is called the \textit{limit solenoid} $\sol$.

nodes.name: solenoid homeomorphism $\mathsf{e}$
nodes.statement:
The two-sided shift on $X^{\mathbb{Z}}$ induces a
homeomorphism $\mathsf{e}:\sol\rightarrow\sol$.

nodes.name: Binary adding machine
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Example.} Consider the transformation $a$ of the space $X^{*}$ over the binary alphabet
$X=\{0,1\}$ defined recursively by the rule
\begin{eqnarray*}
a(0w)=1w \quad \mbox{ and }\quad a(1w)=0a(w)
\end{eqnarray*}
for $w\in X^{*}$. The action of $a$ on the space $X^{*}$ corresponds to addition of one in the
binary numeration system, and therefore the transformation $a$ is called the (binary)
\textit{adding machine}. Indeed, $a(x_1x_2\ldots x_n)=y_1y_2\ldots y_n$ for $x_i,y_i\in X$ if and
only if
\[
1+x_1+2x_2+\ldots +2^{n-1}x_n=y_1+2y_2+\ldots+2^{n-1}y_n \mod 2^{n}.
\]
\begin{figure}
\begin{center}
\psfrag{a}{$a$} \psfrag{a1}{$a^{-1}$} \psfrag{id}{$id$} \psfrag{00}{$(0,0)$} \psfrag{11}{$(1,1)$}
\psfrag{01}{$(0,1)$} \psfrag{10}{$(1,0)$} \epsfig{file=fig2.eps,height=110pt}\caption{The nucleus
of the adding machine} \end{center}
\end{figure}
The group generated by $a$ is the infinite cyclic group, and we have a self-similar action of the
group $\mathbb{Z}\cong\langle a\rangle$ on the space $X^{*}$. This action corresponds to the virtual
endomorphism $\phi:2\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$ given by $\phi(m)=m/2$ and the coset transversal $T=\{0,1\}$
(there is no need to specify the cocycle for abelian groups). The nucleus of the action
$(\mathbb{Z},X^{*})$ is shown in Figure~\ref{fig_AddingMachine}. It follows that two sequences in
$X^{-\omega}\times \mathbb{Z}$ are asymptotically equivalent if and only if they are of the form
\[
\ldots 000\cdot a^{n+1} \approx \ldots 111\cdot a^n \quad \mbox{or} \quad \ldots 001w\cdot a^n
\approx \ldots 110w\cdot a^n
\]
for $w\in X^{*}$ and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. This is the usual identification of binary expansions of real
numbers (but written to the left). Hence the map $\Phi$ given by the rule
\[
\Phi(\ldots x_2x_1\cdot a^n)=n+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \frac{x_i}{2^i},\quad x_i\in X \mbox{ and }
n\in\mathbb{Z},
\]
induces a homeomorphism between the limit $G$-space $\limGs[(\mathbb{Z},X^{*})]$ and the real line
$\mathbb{R}$ with the standard action of $\mathbb{Z}$ by translations. The image of the tile $\mathscr{T}$ under
$\Phi$ is the unit interval $[0,1]$. The limit space $\lims[(\mathbb{Z},X^{*})]$ is homeomorphic to the
unit circle.
nodes.section: 3 Self-similar actions and its limit spaces
nodes.statement_short: The binary adding machine: its limit $G$-space is $\mathbb{R}$, the tile is $[0,1]$ and the limit space is the circle.

nodes.name: measure $\mu$ on the limit $G$-space
nodes.statement:
We consider the uniform
Bernoulli measure $\mu_u$ on the space $X^{-\omega}$ and the counting measure on the group $G$, and we put
the product measure on the space $X^{-\omega}\times G$. The push-forward of this measure under the factor
map $\pi_{\limGs[]}:X^{-\omega}\times G\rightarrow\limGs$ defines the \textit{measure $\mu$ on the limit
$G$-space} $\limGs$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mu$ is the push-forward of uniform Bernoulli times counting measure from $X^{-\omega}\times G$ to the limit $G$-space.

nodes.name: Measures of tiles: scaling, disjointness, self-similarity
nodes.statement: The measures of tiles have the following properties. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mu(\mathscr{T}_v)= |X|^n\cdot\mu(\mathscr{T}_{uv})$ for every $v\in X^{*}$ and $u\in X^n$. \item $\mu(\mathscr{T}_v\cap\mathscr{T}_{v'})=0$ for $v,v'\in X^n, v\neq v'$. \item Let $\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}$ be the measure $\mu$ restricted to the tile $\mathscr{T}$. Then \[ \mu|_{\mathscr{T}}(A)=\sum_{x\in X} \frac{1}{|X|}\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}(\tau_x^{-1}(A)) \] for any Borel set $A\subset\mathscr{T}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Tile measures scale by $|X|^{-n}$, same-level tiles overlap in measure zero, and $\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}$ is self-similar under the $\tau_x$.
conclusions: $\mu(\mathscr{T}_v)= |X|^n\cdot\mu(\mathscr{T}_{uv})$ for every $v\in X^{*}$ and $u\in X^n$.
$\mu(\mathscr{T}_v\cap\mathscr{T}_{v'})=0$ for $v,v'\in X^n, v\neq v'$.
nodes.label: prop_measure lims propert

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10
nodes.statement: Let us show that $\mu(A)\geq |X|\mu(\tau_x(A))$ for any Borel set $A$. Consider sequences which represent points of the sets $A$ and $\tau_x(A)$: \[ \pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}(A)=\bigcup_{g\in G}T_g\cdot g \ \ \Rightarrow \ \ \pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}(\tau_x(A))=\bigcup_{g\in G}T_g g(x)\cdot g|_x. \] It implies \[ \mu(\tau_x(A))\leq \sum_{g\in G} \frac{1}{|X|}\mu_u (T_g)=\frac{1}{|X|}\mu(A). \] By applying this inequality $n$ times we get $|X|^n\mu(\mathscr{T}_v)=|X|^n\mu(\tau_v(\mathscr{T}))\leq\mu(\mathscr{T})$ for $v\in{X}^n$. Since $\mathscr{T}=\cup_{u\in X^n}\mathscr{T}_{u}$ we have that \[ \mu(\mathscr{T})\leq\sum_{u\in X^n}\mu(\mathscr{T}_{u})\leq\sum_{u\in X^n}\frac{1}{|X|^n}\mu(\mathscr{T})=\mu(\mathscr{T}). \] Hence all the above inequalities are actually equalities, $\mu(\mathscr{T})=|X|^n\mu(\mathscr{T}_{u})$ for every $u\in X^n$, and $\mu(\mathscr{T}_u\cap\mathscr{T}_{u'})=0$ for different $u,u'\in X^n$. Notice that since every Borel set $A\subset\mathscr{T}$ can be approximated by unions of tiles of the same level and using items 1 and 2 we have that if $\mu(\tau_x(A))<\varepsilon$ then $\mu(A)<\varepsilon|X|$. It is left to prove item 3. First, let us show that the assertion holds for the tiles $\mathscr{T}_v$. Since the measure $\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}$ is concentrated on the tile $\mathscr{T}$, up to sets of measure zero the set $\tau_x^{-1}(\mathscr{T}_v)$ is equal $\mathscr{T}_u$ if $v=ux$, and is empty if the last letter of $v$ is not $x$. Really, if $t\in\tau_x^{-1}(\mathscr{T}_{ux})$ and $t\in\mathscr{T}_v$ with $v\neq u, |v|=|u|$, then $\tau_x(t)\in\mathscr{T}_{vx}\cap\mathscr{T}_{ux}$ and the measure of such points is zero. Hence \[ \mu|_{\mathscr{T}}(\mathscr{T}_v)=\frac{1}{|X|}\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}(\mathscr{T}_u)=\sum_{x\in X} \frac{1}{|X|}\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}(\tau_x^{-1}(\mathscr{T}_v)). \] Now we can approximate any Borel set by unions of tiles and pass to the limit.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mu(\tau_x(A))\le\mu(A)/|X|$, iterate over level-$n$ tiles to force equalities, then verify self-similarity on tiles and approximate Borel sets.

nodes.name: The tile is the attractor of the $\tau_x$
nodes.statement:
The tile $\mathscr{T}$ of the limit $G$-space $\limGs$ can be considered as the attractor of the iterated
function system $\tau_x$, $x\in X$, i.e.
\[
\mathscr{T}=\bigcup_{x\in X}\tau_x(\mathscr{T}).
\]
conclusions: The tile $\mathscr{T}$ of the limit $G$-space $\limGs$ can be considered as the attractor of the iterated function system $\tau_x$, $x\in X$

nodes.name: $\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}$ is a Hutchinson self-similar measure
nodes.statement:
Hence Proposition~\ref{prop_measure lims propert} item~3 implies that $\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}$ is the
self-similar measure on $\mathscr{T}$ by the standard definition of Hutchinson
(\ref{eqn_self_similar_measure}).
conclusions: $\mu|_{\mathscr{T}}$ is the self-similar measure on $\mathscr{T}$

nodes.name: graph $\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}$ of the nucleus
nodes.statement:
Replacing each label $(x,y)$ by label $x$ in the
nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ we get a strictly right-resolving graph denoted $\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}$ labeled by elements
of $X$, so that we can apply the methods developed in Section~2.

nodes.name: Tile measure equals the measure number of the nucleus
nodes.statement: The measure $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ is equal to the measure number $meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})$ of the nucleus, in particular it is always integer. Moreover, $\mu(\mathscr{T})=1$ if and only if the action satisfies the open set condition.
nodes.statement_short: $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ is the integer measure number of the nucleus graph; it equals 1 exactly under the open set condition.
conclusions: The measure $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ is equal to the measure number $meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})$ of the nucleus, in particular it is always integer.
$\mu(\mathscr{T})=1$ if and only if the action satisfies the open set condition
also_stated_at:
It is proved
in Section~\ref{section_Measures} that the measure $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ is equal to the measure number of
the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$.
nodes.label: theor_tile_measure

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} we have \[ \pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}(\mathscr{T})=\bigcup_{g\in\mathcal{N}}F_g\cdot g^{-1}, \] where the sets $F_g$ are defined using the graph $\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}$ (see Section~2). Thus \[ \mu(\mathscr{T})=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{N}}\mu_u(F_g)=meas(\mathcal{N}), \] which is integer by Theorem~\ref{theor_measure_graph_integer}. Observe that $\mu(\mathscr{T})\geq 1$ because $F_g=X^{-\omega}$ for $g=1\in\mathcal{N}$. If the action satisfies the open set condition then $\mu(\mathscr{T})=meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})=1$ by Corollary~\ref{cor_meas_sum_meas}. Suppose now that the action does not satisfy the open set condition. Then there exists an element $h$ of the nucleus, whose all restrictions are non-trivial. Let $\mathcal{N}_1$ be the set of all restrictions of $h$, and $\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}_1}$ be the corresponding graph. Then by Proposition~\ref{prop cup B_v eq cup F_v} \[ \sum_{g\in\mathcal{N}_1}\mu_u(F_g)=meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}_1})\geq 1. \] Thus $\mu(\mathscr{T})=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{N}}\mu_u(F_g)\geq meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}_1})+\mu_u(F_{g=1})\geq 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the preimage of the tile via nucleus sets $F_g$ and apply Theorem 1; OSC gives 1 by Corollary 4, otherwise a nontrivial restriction-closed subgraph adds at least 1.

nodes.name: Algorithmic computation of the tile measure
nodes.statement: The measure $\mu(\mathscr{T})=meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})$ can be found algorithmically using the remarks after Proposition~\ref{prop_eigenvect_transition_matr}.

nodes.name: The tile covering is a perfect multiple covering
nodes.statement: Every point $x\in\limGs$ is covered by at least $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles. The set $\dot{\limGs}$ of all points $x\in\limGs$, which are covered by exactly $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles, is open and dense in $\limGs$, and its complement has measure $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Every point lies in at least $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles; points in exactly $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles form an open dense set of full measure.
conclusions: Every point $x\in\limGs$ is covered by at least $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles.
The set $\dot{\limGs}$ of all points $x\in\limGs$, which are covered by exactly $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles, is open and dense in $\limGs$, and its complement has measure $0$.
also_stated_at:
Then the
covering $\limGs=\cup_{g\in G}\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ is a perfect multiple covering of multiplicity
$\mu(\mathscr{T})$, i.e. every point of $\limGs$ belongs to at least $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles and almost every
point belongs to precisely $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles.
nodes.label: points_above

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 12
nodes.statement: For each $x\in\limGs$ we define the number $n_x$ of such $g\in G$ that the tile $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ contains $x$. First we prove the inequality. Let $x\in\limGs$ be represented by the pair $w\cdot g$ from $X^{-\omega}\times G$. Then $|V(w)|\geq meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})$ by Theorem~\ref{theor_measure_graph_integer}. If $h\in V(w)$ it means that the sequence $w$ ends in $h$, which by Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} means that there is a sequence $u_h\in X^{-\omega}$ such that $w$ is asymptotically equivalent to $u_h\cdot h$. It follows that $w\cdot g$ is asymptotically equivalent to $u_h\cdot hg$. It means, in turn, that $x$ belongs to the tile $\mathscr{T}\cdot hg$ for every $h\in V(w)$. It follows that $n_x\geq meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})$. Consider the set $\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})$ defined in Lemma~\ref{lemma_set V open dense} using the graph $\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}$, in other words $\mathcal{O}$ is the set of all $w\in X^{-\omega}$ that end in precisely $meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})$ elements of $\mathcal{N}$. By the same considerations as above we see that if $w\cdot g$ represents a point $x$ with $n_x=meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})$ then $|V(w)|=meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})$, that is, $w$ belongs to $\mathcal{O}$. In other words, the set $\mathcal{O}\times G$ is closed under the asymptotic equivalence relation on $X^{-\omega}\times G$, and it is the inverse image of the set $\dot{\limGs}$ under the factor map $\pi_{\limGs[]}$. Since the set $\mathcal{O}\times G$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}\times G$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma_set V open dense}, the same hold for $\dot{\limGs}$ in $\limGs$. The complement of $\dot{\limGs}$ has measure $0$, because the complement of the set $\mathcal{O}$ has measure $0$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma_set V open dense}.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound from $|V(w)|\ge meas$ via nucleus paths; the exact-multiplicity set lifts to $\mathcal{O}\times G$, open dense of full measure by Lemma 1.

nodes.name: The tile boundary has measure zero
nodes.statement: Let $\partial\mathscr{T}$ be the boundary of $\mathscr{T}$. Then $\mu(\partial\mathscr{T})=0$.
assumptions: Let $\partial\mathscr{T}$ be the boundary of $\mathscr{T}$.
conclusions: $\mu(\partial\mathscr{T})=0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 13
nodes.statement: Take $x\in\partial\mathscr{T}$. Suppose that $x$ is covered by exactly $k=\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles. Let $U\subset\dot{\limGs}$ be the neighborhood of $x$ which intersects with finitely many tiles, say with $l\geq k$ tiles. By subtracting any tile that does not contain $x$ we may suppose that $l=k$, that is, $U$ has nonempty intersection only with those tiles that contain $x$. Now, since $x$ is in the boundary of $\mathscr{T}$, there is a point $x'$ in $U$ that is not covered by $\mathscr{T}$ (otherwise $x\in U\subset\mathscr{T}$), thus $x'$ is covered by less than $k$ tiles, contradiction. Hence $\partial\mathscr{T}$ is in the complement of $\dot{\limGs}$ and has measure $0$.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: a boundary point of exact multiplicity would have nearby points covered by fewer than $\mu(\mathscr{T})$ tiles.

nodes.name: Measure of the intersection of two tiles
nodes.statement: Two tiles $\mathscr{T}\cdot g_1$ and $\mathscr{T}\cdot g_2$ for $g_1,g_2\in G$ have nonempty intersection if and only if $g_1g_2^{-1}\in\mathcal{N}$. Let us show how to find the measure of this intersection. By Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} we have \begin{eqnarray*} \pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}((\mathscr{T}\cdot g_1)\cap (\mathscr{T}\cdot g_2))=\bigcup_{{\scriptsize\begin{array}{c} h_1,h_2\in\mathcal{N} \\ g_1g_2^{-1}=h_1h_2^{-1} \end{array}}} (F_{h_1}\cap F_{h_2})\cdot h_1^{-1}g_1, \end{eqnarray*} where the sets $F_g$ are defined using the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$. The word problem in contracting self-similar groups is solvable in polynomial time \cite[Proposition~2.13.10]{self_sim_groups} (one can use the program package \cite{AutomGrp}). The measures of intersections $F_{h_1}\cap F_{h_2}$ can be found for example using method described after Corollary~\ref{cor_meas_gr_rational}.
nodes.statement_short: The measure of $\mathscr{T}g_1\cap\mathscr{T}g_2$ is computed from intersections $F_{h_1}\cap F_{h_2}$ over nucleus pairs with $h_1h_2^{-1}=g_1g_2^{-1}$.
nodes.label: rem_meas_inters_tiles

nodes.name: Existence of self-similar actions with the open set condition
nodes.statement:
It is an interesting open question in what cases we can always choose a self-similar action
which satisfies the open set condition (see \cite{mult_an_self_sim,lag_wang:haar} for the abelian
case and applications to wavelets).

nodes.name: Measure on the limit $G$-space depends only on the virtual endomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $\phi: H\rightarrow G$ be a virtual endomorphism of the group $G$. Let $(G,X^*)$ and $(G,Y^*)$ be the contracting self-similar actions defined respectively by the triples $(\phi,T,C)$ and $(\phi,T',C')$. Then the homeomorphism $\alpha : \limGs[(G,X^*)]\longrightarrow \limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ from Theorem~\ref{theor_limsX hom limsY} preserves measure, i.e. \[ \mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(A))=\mu_{(G,X^*)}(A) \] for any Borel set $A$.
nodes.statement_short: The homeomorphism $\alpha$ between limit $G$-spaces of two actions with the same virtual endomorphism preserves the measure $\mu$.
assumptions: Let $\phi: H\rightarrow G$ be a virtual endomorphism of the group $G$.
Let $(G,X^*)$ and $(G,Y^*)$ be the contracting self-similar actions defined respectively by the triples $(\phi,T,C)$ and $(\phi,T',C')$.
conclusions: the homeomorphism $\alpha : \limGs[(G,X^*)]\longrightarrow \limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ from Theorem~\ref{theor_limsX hom limsY} preserves measure
nodes.label: theor_measure_limGs_invariant

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 14
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{N}$ be the nucleus and $\mathscr{T}$ be the tile of the action $(G,X^{*})$. By Theorem~\ref{theor_tile_measure} and Theorem~\ref{theor_measure_graph_integer} \begin{equation} \mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})=meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|=k\in\mathbb{N}, \end{equation} where $V(w)$ is defined using the graph $\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}$. Consider \[ \pi_Y^{-1}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}))=\bigcup_{g\in G} T_g\cdot g\quad (\mbox{here } T_g\subseteq Y^{-\omega}), \] where $\pi_Y:Y^{-\omega}\times G\rightarrow \limGs$ is the canonical projection. Take $w\in Y^{-\omega}$ and let us prove that there exist at least $k$ elements $g\in G$ such that $w\in T_g$. The tiles $\mathscr{T}\cdot g$ cover the limit $G$-space $\limGs[(G,X^*)]$, and we can find $g\in G$ such that if $x=\alpha^{-1}(y)$ for $y=\pi_{Y}(w\cdot g)\in\limGs[(G,Y^*)]$ then $x$ belongs to the tile $\mathscr{T}$. Then $x$ is represented by the sequence $u\cdot 1$ for $u\in X^{-\omega}$. Equation~(\ref{eqn_theor_meraXY_mu tile }) implies $|V(u)|\geq k$ and so there exist $k$ elements $h_1,\ldots, h_k\in\mathcal{N}$ and sequences $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in X^{-\omega}$ such that for every $i$ there exists a left-infinite path in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ which ends in $h_i$ and is labeled by $(u,u_i)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} \[ x=\pi_X(u\cdot 1)=\pi_X(u_i\cdot h_i)\quad\mbox{ and }\quad x\cdot h_i^{-1}\in\mathscr{T} \] for every $i=1,\ldots, k$. Then \[ \pi_Y(w\cdot gh_i^{-1})=\pi_Y(w\cdot g)h_i^{-1}=y\cdot h_i^{-1}=\alpha(x\cdot h_i^{-1})\in\alpha(\mathscr{T}) \] and thus $w\in T_{gh_i^{-1}}$ for all $i=1,\ldots, k$. Let $\chi_{T_g}$ be the characteristic function of the set $T_g$. Then $\sum_{g\in G}\chi_{T_g}(x)\geq k$ for almost all $x$. Integrating we get $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}))=\sum_{g\in G} \mu_u(T_g)\geq k=\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})$. Let us now show that $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}_v))\leq\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T}_v)$ for any $v\in X^*$. Indeed, let $n=|v|$, then it follows from Theorem \ref{theor_limsX hom limsY} that $\alpha(\mathscr{T}_v)=\alpha(\tau_v(\mathscr{T}))=\tau_u(\alpha(\mathscr{T}))g$ for some word $u\in Y^n$ and $g\in G$. Thus \begin{eqnarray*} \mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}_v))&=&\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\tau_u(\alpha(\mathscr{T})))\leq\frac{1}{|X|^n}\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}))=\\ &=&\frac{1}{|X|^n}\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})=\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T}_v). \end{eqnarray*} Let us prove that $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu_{(G,X^*)}$. Indeed, let $\mu_{(G,X^*)}(A)<\varepsilon$, $\pi^{-1}_{X}(A)=\cup_g T_g\cdot g$. Then $\sum_g\mu_u(T_g)<\varepsilon$. It follows that there exist $v_{i,g}\in X^*$ such that $T_g\subset\cup_iX^{-\omega} v_{i,g}$ and $\sum_{i,g}|X|^{-|v_{i,g}|}<\varepsilon$. Then $A\subset\cup_{i,g}\mathscr{T}_{v_{i,g}}\cdot g$, and we have that $\sum_{i,g}\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T}_{v_{i,g}})<\varepsilon\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})$. Then $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(A))\leq\sum\mu_{(G,Y^*)}(\alpha(\mathscr{T}_{v_{i,g}}))\leq\sum\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T}_{v_{i,g}})<\varepsilon\mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})$. Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, we are done. We will now prove that $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha\leq\mu_{(G,X^*)}$. Since both $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha$ and $\mu_{(G,X^*)}$ are invariant under multiplication by $g\in G$ it suffices to prove this inequality for sets $A\subset\mathscr{T}$. Since any Borel $A$ is a union of a closed set and a set of arbitrarily small measure, it suffices to prove the inequality for closed sets, as $\mu_{(G,Y^*)}\circ\alpha$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu_{(G,X^*)}$ by above. So let $A\subset\mathscr{T}$ be a closed set. For each $n$, let $A_n$ be the union of all tiles $\mathscr{T}_v,v\in X^n,$ that have non-empty intersection with $A$. Let us show that $A=\cap_n A_n$. Suppose $x\in\cap A_n$, and $x$ is not in $A$. Then for each $n$ there is $v_n\in X^n$ such that $\mathscr{T}_{v_n}$ has nonempty intersection with $A$ and $x\in\mathscr{T}_{v_n}$. It follows that $x$ has some representation $u_nv_n\in X^{-\omega}$. Since the number of such representations is finite, we may choose subsequence $n_k$ such that $v_{n_k}$ is the beginning of some word $v\in X^{-\omega}$. Since $A$ is compact it follows that $A$ has nonempty intersection with $\cap_k\mathscr{T}_{v_{n_k}}$, thus $\cap_k\mathscr{T}_{v_{n_k}}$ contains at least two points, which is impossible. Since $A_n$ is the union of some tiles of level $n$, which are disjoint up to sets of measure $0$, the inequality also holds for all $A_n$. Going to the limit, we get the inequality for $A$. By interchanging $X$ and $Y$ we get the reverse inequality, and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\mu_Y(\alpha(\mathscr{T}))\ge\mu_X(\mathscr{T})$ via multiplicity, then $\mu_Y\circ\alpha\le\mu_X$ on tiles, absolute continuity and closed sets; symmetry gives equality. The key step approximates closed sets by unions of level-$n$ tiles.

nodes.name: Tile measure as minimal $|V(w)|$
nodes.statement: \mu_{(G,X^*)}(\mathscr{T})=meas(\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}})=\min_{w\in X^{-\omega}} |V(w)|=k\in\mathbb{N},
nodes.label: eqn_theor_meraXY_mu tile

nodes.name: Uniform measure is essential in Theorem 14
nodes.statement: It is important in the theorem that we take the uniform Bernoulli measure on $X^{-\omega}$. The problem is that the homeomorphism $\alpha$ may change the Bernoulli measure with a non-uniform weight to a measure that is not Bernoulli.

nodes.name: self-similar measure $\mathsf{m}$ on the limit space
nodes.statement:
The push-forward
of the uniform Bernoulli measure $\mu_u$ under the factor map $\pi_{\lims[]}:X^{-\omega}\rightarrow\lims$
defines the \textit{self-similar measure $\mathsf{m}$ on the limit space} $\lims$.
nodes.definiendum: self-similar measure $\mathsf{m}$ on the limit space

nodes.name: The shift is measure preserving
nodes.statement:
The shift $\mathsf{s}$ is a measure-preserving
transformation of $\lims$.
conclusions: The shift $\mathsf{s}$ is a measure-preserving transformation of $\lims$.

nodes.name: set $\mathcal{U}$
nodes.statement:
Consider the set $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{N})$ of all sequences $w\in X^{-\omega}$ with the property
that every left-infinite path in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(w,w)$ ends in $1$.

nodes.name: set $\mathcal{U}^*$
nodes.statement:
Define
$\mathcal{U}^*$ as the set of finite words that satisfy the same condition.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{U}$ is open, dense, of full measure and saturated
nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{U}$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}$, and $\mu_p(\mathcal{U})=1$. For each $w\in \mathcal{U}$ there is a beginning of $w$ that belongs to $\mathcal{U}^*$, and $\mathcal{U}=\cup_{w\in\mathcal{U}^*}X^{-\omega} w$. The sets $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{U}\times G$ are closed under the asymptotic equivalence relation on $X^{-\omega}$ and $X^{-\omega}\times G$ respectively.
conclusions: The set $\mathcal{U}$ is open and dense in $X^{-\omega}$, and $\mu_p(\mathcal{U})=1$.
The sets $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{U}\times G$ are closed under the asymptotic equivalence relation on $X^{-\omega}$ and $X^{-\omega}\times G$ respectively.
nodes.label: lemma U_open_dense_meas1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Construct the graph $\Gamma$ with the elements of $\mathcal{N}$ as vertices, for each edge labeled by $(x,x)$ in $\mathcal{N}$ we have the edge in $\Gamma$ with the same starting and end vertices, and labeled by $x$; and for each edge in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(x,y)$ for $x\neq y$ there is an edge in $\Gamma$ with the same starting vertex that ends in the trivial element and labeled by $x$. Then the set $\mathcal{U}$ coincides with the set $\mathcal{O}(\Gamma)$. Indeed, $h\in V_{\Gamma}(w)$ if and only if there is a path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(w,w)$ that ends in $h$, thus $w\in\mathcal{U}$ if and only if $V_{\Gamma}(w)=\{1\}$. For every nontrivial element $h\in\mathcal{N}$ there exists a word $v\in X^{*}$ such that $h(v)\neq v$. It follows that there exists a path in the graph $\Gamma$ from $h$ to $1$. Hence the component $\{1\}$ is the only strongly connected component of the graph $\Gamma$ without outgoing edges. By Corollary~\ref{cor_meas_sum_meas} the measure number of $\Gamma$ is $1$, and $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{O}(\Gamma)$. The first statement of the lemma now follows from Lemma~\ref{lemma_set V open dense}. Let us show that the set $\mathcal{U}$ is closed under the asymptotic equivalence relation (then the set $\mathcal{U}\times G$ is also closed). It is sufficient to show that if there is a path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(u,v)$ and $u\in\mathcal{U}$ ($v\in\mathcal{U}$) then $v\in\mathcal{U}$ ($u\in\mathcal{U}$). Let the path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(u,v)$ end in $h$. It follows that $u$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot h$. Suppose there is a path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(v,v)$ that ends in $g$. It follows that $v$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot g$. Thus $u$ is asymptotically equivalent to $v\cdot gh$ which is asymptotically equivalent to $u\cdot h^{-1}gh$. By definition, there is a path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(u,u)$ which ends in $h^{-1}gh$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$ we get $h^{-1}gh=1$, thus $g=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Encode $\mathcal{U}$ as $\mathcal{O}(\Gamma)$ for a graph with measure number 1 and apply Lemma 1; saturation via conjugating nucleus paths.

nodes.name: Almost every point has $|X|$ preimages under $\mathsf{s}$
nodes.statement: Almost every point of $\lims$ has precisely $|X|$ preimages under~$\mathsf{s}$.
conclusions: Almost every point of $\lims$ has precisely $|X|$ preimages under~$\mathsf{s}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 15
nodes.statement: Since every point of $\lims$ has at most $|X|$ preimages under $\mathsf{s}$, it is enough to show that for almost every $w\in X^{-\omega}$ the map $\pi_{\lims[]}:\sigma^{-1}(w)\rightarrow\mathsf{s}^{-1}(\pi_{\lims[]}(w))$ is one-to-one. Suppose that for some $w\in X^{-\omega}$ and $x\neq y$ in $X$ we have $\pi_{\lims[]}(wx)=\pi_{\lims[]}(wy)$. It follows that $wx,wy$ are asymptotically equivalent, thus there is a left-infinite path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(wx,wy)$. It follows that the prefix of this path labeled by $(w,w)$ must end in the nontrivial element, so $w\not\in\mathcal{U}$. Since $\mu_u(\mathcal{U})=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma U_open_dense_meas1}, we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Coinciding images of $wx, wy$ force a nontrivial nucleus path labeled $(w,w)$, so $w\notin\mathcal{U}$, a null set by Lemma 2.

nodes.name: Factor map is a homeomorphism on tiles $\mathscr{T}_u$, $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$
nodes.statement: Let $\rho$ be the factor map $\limGs\rightarrow\lims$. Then for any $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ the restriction $\rho|_{\mathscr{T}_u}:\mathscr{T}_u\rightarrow\mathsf{T}_u$ is a homeomorphism, $\rho^{-1}(\mathsf{T}_u)=\sqcup_{g\in G}\mathscr{T}_u\cdot g$.
assumptions: Let $\rho$ be the factor map $\limGs\rightarrow\lims$.
for any $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$
conclusions: the restriction $\rho|_{\mathscr{T}_u}:\mathscr{T}_u\rightarrow\mathsf{T}_u$ is a homeomorphism
$\rho^{-1}(\mathsf{T}_u)=\sqcup_{g\in G}\mathscr{T}_u\cdot g$
nodes.label: x_j_homeo

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 16
nodes.statement: By definition, the map $\rho|_{\mathscr{T}_u}:\mathscr{T}_u\rightarrow\mathsf{T}_u$ is surjective, and $\mathscr{T}_u$ is compact. Hence in order to prove that $\rho$ is a homeomorphism it is left to show that $\rho$ is injective on $\mathscr{T}_u$. Take $x,y\in\mathscr{T}_u$, and let $wu\in X^{-\omega}$ represent $x$ and $vu\in X^{-\omega}$ represent $y$. Suppose that $\rho(x)=\rho(y)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop_asympt_Moore_diagr} it means that there is a left-infinite path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(wu,vu)$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$, this path must end in $1$. It follows, that $wu$ and $vu$ represent the same point of the tile $\mathscr{T}_u$, and $x=y$. To prove the second claim, take $x\in\mathscr{T}_u\cdot g\cap\mathscr{T}_u\cdot g'$. Then $x$ is represented by two asymptotically equivalent sequences $wu\cdot g$ and $w'u\cdot g'$. It follows that there is a path in the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(u,u)$ which ends in $g'g^{-1}$. Then $g=g'$ since $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Compactness reduces to injectivity, which follows since nucleus paths labeled through $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ end in 1.

nodes.name: Projection $\limGs\to\lims$ is a covering up to null sets
nodes.statement: The projection $\limGs\rightarrow\lims$ is a covering map up to sets of measure zero.
conclusions: The projection $\limGs\rightarrow\lims$ is a covering map up to sets of measure zero.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 17
nodes.statement: Consider the sets $\tilde{\limGs}=\pi_{\limGs[]}(\mathcal{U}\times G)$ and $\tilde{\lims}=\pi_{\lims[]}(\mathcal{U})$. It follows that $\tilde{\limGs}/G=\tilde{\lims}$. Since the set $\mathcal{U}$ has measure $1$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma U_open_dense_meas1}, the complements of $\mathcal{U}\times G$, of $\tilde{\limGs}$, and of $\tilde{\lims}$ have measure $0$. Since the group $G$ acts properly on $\limGs$, the same holds for $\tilde{\limGs}$. It is left to prove the freeness. Suppose $x\cdot g=x$ for $x\in\tilde{\limGs}$ and $g\in G$. Let $u\cdot h$ be a representative of $x$ in $X^{-\omega}\times G$. It follows that $u\cdot hg$ is asymptotically equivalent to $u\cdot h$, thus there is a path in $\mathcal{N}$ labeled by $(u,u)$ that ends in $h^{-1}gh$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$ we have $g=1$. Hence the projection $\tilde{\limGs}\rightarrow\tilde{\lims}$ is a covering map, and the statement follows.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to the full-measure saturated set from $\mathcal{U}$, where $G$ acts properly and freely, so the projection is a covering.

nodes.name: quotient measure
nodes.statement:
Let $(\limGs[],
u)$ be a locally compact measure space, the group $G$ acts freely and properly
discontinuously on $\limGs[]$ by homeomorphisms, and the measure $
u$ is $G$-invariant. There is a
unique measure $
u_{*}$ on the quotient space $\limGs[]/G$, called the 	extit{quotient measure},
with the property that if $U$ is an open subset of $\limGs[]$ such that $Ug\cap Uh=\emptyset$ for
all $g,h\in G$, $g
eq h$, then $
u_{*}(U/G)=
u(U)$.
nodes.statement_short: For a free, properly discontinuous measure-preserving action, the quotient measure assigns $U/G$ the measure of a set $U$ with disjoint translates.

nodes.name: Quotient of $\mu$ is the self-similar measure $\mathsf{m}$
nodes.statement: The quotient measure $\mu_{*}$ of the limit $G$-space $(\limGs,\mu)$ coincides with the measure $\mathsf{m}$ on the limit space $\lims$.
conclusions: The quotient measure $\mu_{*}$ of the limit $G$-space $(\limGs,\mu)$ coincides with the measure $\mathsf{m}$ on the limit space $\lims$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 18
nodes.statement: Consider the sets $\tilde{\lims}$ and $\tilde{\limGs}$ of full measure from the previous theorem. For every $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ we have $\mathsf{T}_u\subset\tilde{\lims}$, $\mathscr{T}_u\cdot g\subset\tilde{\limGs}$ for every $g\in G$, and $\rho^{-1}(\mathsf{T}_u)=\bigsqcup_{g\in G} \mathscr{T}_u\cdot g$ by Proposition~\ref{x_j_homeo}. Since $\tilde{\lims}=\cup_{u\in\mathcal{U}^*}\mathsf{T}_u$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma U_open_dense_meas1} it suffices to show that for any $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$ the restriction of $\mu_{*}$ on $\mathsf{T}_u$ is equal to the restriction of $\mathsf{m}$. Take a Borel set $A\subset\mathscr{T}_u$ and consider its preimage $\pi^{-1}_{\limGs[]}(A)=\sqcup_{g\in\mathcal{N}} A_g\cdot g$. Then $\pi^{-1}_{\lims[]}(\rho(A))=\sqcup_{g\in\mathcal{N}} A_g$. Here the union is disjoint because if $w\in{A_g\cap{}A_h}$ then $w\cdot g$ and $w\cdot h$ are asymptotically equivalent to $vu$ and $v'u$ respectively, for some $v,v'\in X^{-\omega}$. It follows that $vu\cdot g^{-1}$ is equivalent to $v'u\cdot h^{-1}$. Since $u\in\mathcal{U}$, $g=h$. Hence \[ \mathsf{m}(\rho(A))=\mu_u(\pi^{-1}_{\lims[]}(\rho(A)))=\mu_u(\sqcup_{g\in\mathcal{N}} A_g)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{N}}\mu_u(A_g). \] By the property of the quotient measure \[ \mu_{*}(\rho(A))=\mu(A)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{N}}\mu_u(A_g)=\mathsf{m}(\rho(A)). \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to tiles $\mathsf{T}_u$, $u\in\mathcal{U}^*$, and compare both measures on preimages, which are disjoint by the choice of $u$.
